{{Short description|Concept in linear algebra}}
In [[linear algebra]], a '''reducing subspace''' <math>W</math> of a [[linear map]] <math>T:V\to V</math> from a [[Hilbert space]] <math>V</math> to itself is an [[invariant subspace]] of <math>T</math> whose [[orthogonal complement]] <math>W^\perp</math> is also an invariant subspace of <math>T.</math> That is, <math>T(W) \subseteq W</math> and <math>T(W^\perp) \subseteq W^\perp.</math> One says that the [[linear subspace|subspace]] <math>W</math> '''reduces''' the map <math>T.</math>

One says that a linear map is '''reducible''' if it has a [[linear subspace#Definition|nontrivial]] reducing subspace. Otherwise one says it is '''irreducible'''.

If <math>V</math> is of finite [[dimension (vector space)|dimension]] <math>r</math> and <math>W</math> is a reducing subspace of the map <math>T:V\to V</math> represented under [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] <math>B</math> by matrix <math>M \in\R^{r\times r}</math> then <math>M</math> can be expressed as the sum

<math display=block> M = P_W M P_W + P_{W^\perp} M P_{W^\perp}</math>

where <math>P_W \in\R^{r\times r}</math> is the matrix of the [[orthogonal projection]] from <math>V</math> to <math>W</math> and <math>P_{W^\perp} = I - P_{W}</math> is the matrix of the projection onto <math>W^\perp.</math><ref>{{cite book|author=R. Dennis Cook|title=An Introduction to Envelopes : Dimension Reduction for Efficient Estimation in Multivariate Statistics|publisher=Wiley|year=2018|page=7}}</ref>  (Here <math>I \in \R^{r\times r}</math> is the [[identity matrix]].)

Furthermore, <math>V</math> has an [[orthonormal basis]] <math>B'</math> with a subset that is an orthonormal basis of <math>W</math>. If <math>Q \in \R^{r\times r}</math> is the [[change of basis|transition matrix]] from <math>B</math> to <math>B'</math> then with respect to <math>B'</math> the matrix <math>Q^{-1}MQ</math> representing <math>T</math> is a [[block-diagonal matrix]]

<math display=block>Q^{-1}MQ = \left[ \begin{array}{cc} A & 0 \\ 0 & B \end{array} \right] </math>

with <math> A\in\R^{d\times d},</math> where <math> d= \dim W</math>, and <math> B\in\R^{(r-d)\times(r-d)}.</math>
